text: Herat announced itself before the eye found any wall - a green so sudden after the Farah road's thin channels that Farrukh's caravan guide, a Herati by birth, laughed out loud at his own relief. The Hari Rud ran wide and steady here, feeding orchards and fields that had outlasted every dynasty that had ever claimed them, and the city itself sat in the middle of all that green like a fact nobody had gotten around to arguing with yet. Bost had been a palace pretending to be a market. Herat was simply a city - the biggest, Farrukh understood without being told, since Ghazni itself.

The Hari Rud ran wide and steady here, feeding orchards and fields that had outlasted every dynasty that had ever claimed them, and the city itself sat in the middle of all that green like a fact nobody had gotten around to arguing with yet. Bost had been a palace pretending to be a market. Herat was simply a city - the biggest, Farrukh understood without being told, since Ghazni itself. It was somewhere in the first mile of that green, with water running audibly on both sides of the track, that he thought about the keeper's book at the last post - the one nobody read, that went up in a bundle twice a year to a room where it was put with the other bundles. The room was in here somewhere. Herat was where things came to be written down, which was the entire reason a family out of a village he would never see was walking two days toward it, and the reason his own name now stood in a small tired hand above a line naming them, their village and their errand. He was bringing two names into this city, then. One was in his satchel, had cost him good silver in Farah, and could not be checked. The other had cost him nothing whatever, had not been his to give, and had gone on ahead of him.

text: It did not take an afternoon to learn that Herat struck its own coin - one of six mints still answering to the Sultan, the guide said, with the particular pride of a man reciting a fact about his home he'd repeated to a thousand strangers before Farrukh. It took rather less time to notice the other thing everyone in the bazaar seemed to be discussing in lowered voices: a muster, called sooner and thinner than anyone remembered the last one being, men going to garrison duty who'd expected another season free of it.

choices.text: Let the garrison gate draw you first.

text: An old soldier sat by the garrison gate doing the particular kind of nothing men do when they've been told to wait and given no further instruction - watching new levies shuffle through with the flat expression of someone who has seen this exact scene often enough that the details have stopped mattering to him individually. Farrukh asked, since the man seemed willing to be asked things, what all the hurry was for.

"Hurry." The old soldier said the word like it tasted wrong. "I mustered here myself, boy, fifteen years gone now - when the young prince who's Sultan today first called men up in this very yard, before he'd worn the title a season. That muster had banners, had a march worth remembering, had somewhere real to go and something real to be marching toward." He nodded at the {{hashar|hashar}} shuffling past - farmers and shopkeepers pressed into service rather than soldiers bred to it. "This is a man patching a roof with whatever's on hand because he can't wait for proper tile. Nobody's said the word Seljuk to me directly. Nobody needs to." He didn't say anything further, and didn't seem to expect Farrukh to either.

choices.text: Let it lie. He wasn't asking for an answer.
Tell him what the riders carried as far as Ghazni.

text: Herat's bazaar ran long enough that a man could lose an entire day just walking its length without transacting a single dirham - dyers, ironworkers, a street that smelled entirely of saffron, and, threaded through all of it, the particular hush of stalls where actual silver changed hands rather than goods, run by men who weighed coin for a living the way Mihran had in Bost, except here with a mint's own authority standing behind whatever they said a coin was worth.

Further down from the money-changers' stalls stood the building the whole bazaar's silver eventually answered to - low, heavily guarded, its yard stacked with more sacks of raw metal than finished coin. This was the mint itself, one of the Sultan's six, the thing that had made Ardashir's rate and everyone else's meaningful rather than merely agreed-upon. A line of merchants waited outside longer than any of them looked pleased about, clutching worn coin they wanted restruck clean.

choices.text: Ask what's holding up the line.
It's not your business today. Move on.

text: "Used to turn coin around in a season," the man nearest the gate said, not looking especially eager to be overheard saying it. "Now it's closer to half a year, and getting worse, not better." He didn't say why, and didn't need to - every silver dirham the mint restruck was silver the muster wasn't currently spending, and a garrison calling men up sooner and thinner than usual had first claim on whatever metal moved through this city at all.

Farrukh found the one the road's own gossip had already half-pointed him toward before he'd finished asking - a sarraf named Ardashir, older than Mihran, quieter than Umm-Kavus, running a stall so plain and so trusted that half the caravan trade passing through Herat used no other scale. He took Farrukh's coin for a first, small exchange without comment, weighed it, and named a rate that was, Farrukh judged, exactly fair and not a hair more generous than that.

After Farah, where the honest channel had cost him more than the other one would have and been worth it anyway, a rate that was exactly fair and not a hair more came as something close to relief. He had stopped expecting generosity. He had not stopped needing to know where he stood.

text: He offered to take Farrukh's travel-worn coin off his hands - foreign mintings, clipped edges, the ordinary wreckage of a long road - and give him clean Herat silver in exchange, at a rate that discounted for the wear rather more heavily than Farrukh's own eye judged fair.

choices.text: Walk away, keep the old coin.

text: Farrukh took the rate without argument. Ardashir counted out the clean silver with the same unhurried precision he'd used to name the discount in the first place, and said nothing further about it - a man who had made his offer honestly and expected to be dealt with the same way in return.

Farrukh pointed out, as evenly as he could manage, that the discount ran heavier than the coins' actual wear justified. Ardashir looked at him for a moment with something that might have been mild interest. "It does," he agreed, entirely unbothered. "Most men don't notice, or don't say so if they do. What would you have it be instead?"

Farrukh pushed harder than the moment strictly called for, and got a better rate for it - a smaller one than he'd hoped, and a longer silence from Ardashir afterward than the transaction itself required. Coin was coin. Whatever he'd spent to get it back was harder to weigh.

Farrukh decided the worn coin would spend well enough elsewhere and declined the exchange. Ardashir shrugged, entirely untroubled either way, and went back to whatever he'd been doing before Farrukh's shadow had fallen across his stall.
Farrukh lingered a moment longer than the transaction required, the way a man does when he has a second, harder question waiting behind the first easy one.

"You're not here for silver," Ardashir said, before Farrukh had found a way to raise it himself. "Men who are, don't linger." He named a fee, plainly, for sending word through the correspondents he kept in cities a caravan guide wouldn't think to ask about - the kind of service, he made clear without quite saying so, that existed for exactly the sort of question Farrukh hadn't asked yet.

choices.text: Decide you don't need the service.

text: Farrukh paid what he asked, without argument, the same way he'd learned to pay Umm-Kavus in Farah - and watched something in Ardashir's manner ease by the same small fraction it had eased in hers.

Farrukh tried the fee the way he'd tried the exchange rate - reasonably, without heat. Ardashir's expression didn't change, but he named a slightly lower figure, the kind of movement that cost him nothing and told Farrukh nothing either, except that the door hadn't closed.

Farrukh accepted the reduction and paid it, and let the matter rest there. It was, he judged, exactly the right amount of pressing - enough to show he wasn't being careless with his father's remaining coin, not so much that it read as anything other than ordinary bazaar custom.

Farrukh pressed a second time, the way he had at the exchange rate, and this time Ardashir's patience visibly thinned. He gave the reduction anyway - a sarraf's professional habit outlasting his personal irritation - but the ease that had been building between them closed over like a door shutting quietly rather than being slammed.

Farrukh decided the fee wasn't worth what it bought and said so, and Ardashir took the refusal exactly as evenly as he'd taken everything else - a man who sold a service, not a man invested in anyone buying it. It left the door to Rayy no more open than Farrukh's own nerve would make it, a few minutes from now, without a paid pretext to lean on.
Whatever Ardashir made of him after two rounds of ordinary bazaar business, Farrukh had run out of pretexts for lingering a third time without simply asking.

Farrukh laid it out as plainly as he could manage - the suftaja, the second mark Mihran had recognized and refused to fully explain, the house in Rayy his father's accounts should never have mentioned at all. Ardashir listened without once looking up from the coins he was still, out of habit, sorting.

When he finally did look up, it was with the same particular stillness Farrukh had seen twice already on this road - a man doing the arithmetic of how much a stranger's trustworthiness was actually worth, weighed against what the honest answer might cost him if he'd guessed wrong.

"I could tell you what I actually know," Ardashir said at last, "or I could tell you the version of it that's safe for both of us regardless of who you turn out to be. Which one you get isn't really my decision to make anymore. It's whatever you've already shown me, added up."

choices.text: Ask him plainly, one merchant to another.
Remind him what you've shown him, fairly, since you arrived.

text: "The house had trouble," Ardashir said, choosing his words the way a man picks a path across a floor he doesn't trust. "Trouble tied to things that happened in Rayy a while back - things men in my trade learned not to discuss above a whisper, even now. Your father's paper is a piece of that trouble, passed down further than anyone probably meant it to travel. That's what I can safely give you." It was, Farrukh understood, exactly as much as a cautious stranger owed another cautious stranger, and not one word more.

"Six years ago," Ardashir said, "Rayy had a ruler of its own house - the last of the old Buyid line, a man named Majd al-Dawla - until your Sultan's father took the city and put him somewhere comfortable and permanent in Ghazni instead. That was the political half of it. The other half happened the same year: men were crucified in Rayy's streets for belonging to a network the state called dangerous enough to kill for - {{dai|da'i}}, missionaries for a cause based in Cairo, funded from Cairo, answerable to nobody the Sultan recognized as legitimate. What's left of both collapses - the old house's money, and whatever survived of that network - didn't vanish. It went quiet, and it went underground, and some of it apparently still moves, carefully, through paper like your father's. I don't know why he was carrying it. I don't think you'll like finding out, whenever you do."

Farrukh walked back through Herat's long bazaar without seeing much of it, turning the shape of what he now knew over in his hands like a coin he couldn't yet tell was genuine. His father had never so much as mentioned Rayy at the dinner table, had never once hinted at the shape of the trouble he was leaving behind him - and yet here it was, folded into a debt Farrukh had sworn at a graveside to carry without knowing what, exactly, he'd agreed to be responsible for. Avicenna's floating man, stripped of every borrowed sense, was still supposed to know he existed. Farrukh was beginning to suspect a man could know considerably less than that about the debts he'd sworn to.

That night, before he let himself sleep, Farrukh took out the ledger again and added a second entry beneath the first - not a sum, but the shape of what he now knew: a name, a city, and trouble older than either. It was becoming, he noticed without quite deciding to notice it, a habit rather than a single strange gesture at a caravanserai table - the beginning of whatever accounting he was actually keeping, as distinct from the one his father had left behind him to settle.

He was awake and dressed well before the muster's own working hours began, the timing no accident - a man carrying anything worth hiding wanted the gate at its quietest, not its busiest. Even so, the signs of it reached him before he'd cleared the courtyard: a string of requisitioned pack animals walked past under guard by soldiers who looked barely rested themselves, a runner sent to wake a household two doors down for reasons nobody said aloud, the particular hush of a city bracing for a morning it hadn't chosen the shape of. None of it touched him directly. All of it reminded him, more thoroughly than Ardashir's careful words ever had, that trouble serious enough for a careful man to whisper about, rather than admit outright, didn't need to announce itself twice.

choices.text: Move the paper somewhere less obvious than where it's ridden since Ghazni.
Leave it exactly where it's always been. Moving it now would only teach your own hands there was something to fear.

text: The Hari Rud's green went on for most of a morning west of Herat, which was long enough for Farrukh to stop admiring it and start reading it, and what he read did not sit well. A field of millet had been cut a good three weeks before the ear would have filled, cut low and cut by hand, the stubble left ragged in the way stubble is left ragged when a great many people who do not ordinarily cut a field cut all of it in one afternoon. The threshing floor beyond had been swept down to the packed clay, and swept again, and even the chaff-heap that a household leaves at the edge of its own floor to see the winter out had been taken up and carried off. In the orchard the fruit was still on the branch, pomegranates split open where they hung and nobody troubling about them. And at the head of the plot the channel had been dammed off with turf and beaten earth, dry to the bottom, in the one season of the year when a man puts water on ground he means to sow. His guide, a Herati, looked at the whole of it and said nothing whatever, being a Herati, and having considerably more practice than Farrukh at not remarking on what a muster did to the country he came from.

choices.text: The muster's men came through here with carts, took the year off this village, and went back to Herat.
Nobody carted this anywhere. The households cut it themselves, green, and they are carrying it in on their own backs.

text: They were on the next floor down the road, a dozen of them in the shade of its wall, and they got to their feet when the caravan came up - not out of any alarm, but because people resting on somebody else's threshing floor get up when they are looked at. Two old men, some women, four children, and the load: bundles of millet cut green and tied with twisted straw, and sacks of floor-sweepings made up to a weight. It was owed, they explained, and they explained it in the order the clerk had explained it to them. The muster had taken eleven men and nine pack animals out of their village, lawfully, with the marks set against all twenty of them in a book, and had then assessed the village for the keep of the nine as far as the first stage - delivery to the yards at Herat, at the village's own charge. The animals had gone with their harness, harness being a part of a beast. So there was no rope left in the village, and nothing to carry anything on, and the eleven men who would have carried it were the eleven men in the book. They wanted nothing from him. They said so twice, unprompted, and then stood in the road while he decided.

choices.text: Cut cord and sacking off your own loads and set it down by the bundles before anyone has to ask for it.
Give them what rope and sacking the caravan can spare, once they ask.
Wish them a short road, and go on west.

text: It was the older of the two old men who asked, and he did it in stages, the way a man asks who has settled in advance on being refused. First, whether Farrukh read - the slip the clerk had left with them was in a hand nobody in the village could make anything of beyond the seal, and they had been carrying it four days without knowing what it said about them. Then, once Farrukh had read it out to him, the rest of it: that green fodder weighs at the village and weighs less at the gate, everybody knew that, the drying went out of it on the road; that the Herat scale would therefore find them short of the figure on the slip; and that short was a word which meant something particular once it was in a book. Would Farrukh write out, in a merchant's hand, what had left the village, and the weight it had left at, and that he had seen the load himself on the road at such a place. He offered his own reckoning of the weight, which Farrukh had no way on earth of checking, and did not pretend otherwise. Farrukh stood there holding a strip of somebody else's paper and was aware that he had spent the previous evening deciding where in his pack to keep a different one.

Would Farrukh write out, in a merchant's hand, what had left the village and the weight it had left at, and that he had seen the load himself on the road at such a place. He gave his own reckoning of the weight unpressed and undressed, and Farrukh had no way on earth of checking it. That was the whole of the difference. A quarter of an hour of cord had bought him a man who no longer expected to be refused, and a refusal now would be a thing taken back rather than a thing withheld.

choices.text: Write it out for them. A weight you cannot check is still the only weight anybody will ever have.
Read the slip out to them again, properly, and tell him plainly you will not put your hand to a weight you did not weigh.

text: The clerk was going the other way, east, and Farrukh understood the significance of that before the man had finished being polite about the caravan. He was working the villages back in toward Herat with two of the muster's riders for company and a book he did not put down in order to talk, and he was, he said, reconciling: what had been assessed on the outward circuit against what the yards had actually taken in, the two figures having failed to agree by a margin his superiors had lately begun to take an interest in. He wanted the caravan's origin and its load, which was a formality, and then he wanted to know what Farrukh had passed on the road behind him - fodder moving, and how much of it, and out of which villages, and whether the floors he had gone by were clear. It was a fair question, put by a man entirely entitled to put it, and answering it would cost Farrukh nothing at all: no fee, no delay, no name of his own written down anywhere. It would only mean that a man with a book, riding east, would know what he was looking for a day before he would otherwise have met it standing in the road.

It was a fair question, and his to put. The difficulty was that the true answer was no longer only about them. A good deal of what was holding those bundles together was cord off Farrukh's own loads, cut that morning, and there was no road at all from that morning to this man's page except through Farrukh's own mouth. The clerk was riding east with nothing whatever to tell him otherwise. A merchant who mentioned that he had furnished the carriage would find his caravan's name set down beside the village's while the man was about it - and saying nothing would still cost him nothing. That was somehow the worse of the two.

choices.text: Tell him what you saw. He is reconciling a book, not hunting anybody.
Tell him the road behind you was your own business and nobody else's.

text: He left Herat before the muster drums had found their full rhythm, west toward Pushang and whatever came after it, carrying more of Rayy's trouble than he'd arrived with, dangerous in roughly the proportion Ardashir had warned him it would be.
